title: Doubling tuba and string bass in the theater band
summary: He jumped to tuba when pit music got too hard, and talks of how Morton varied the rhythm texture on records.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Well, were you doubling tuba and bass?
Yeah, that's just when I started doubling in the Met. See, when music get too tough, you know, for the string bass, I'd jump on the tuba.
Oh, really? It was easier to read the parts on tuba?

Yeah, because, see, I was a freshman on the string bass, you know. And some of them bass parts, you know, them standard tunes, and -- you know, what you call music you're playing for the pictures is heavy stuff.
Guys were jamming on the job.

You know, listening to these records, I've noticed not only on the Morton records, but on other records of this time, that instead of the whole rhythm section playing constantly throughout something, like we do now, that -- well, like Jelly would cut out -- well, there was an alto solo where there was just guitar, banjo, whatever he was playing at the time, and Jelly on the piano, and Baby Dodds. You didn't play on like 16 bars.

And then -- then everybody'd come back in, then there would be another section with maybe just drums and piano, and clarinet. To change the texture of the rhythm section. Was that a common thing back in the twenties?
I don't know, I never experienced that. Exception with Jelly. You know, on recording.
Yeah. Louie used to do that on some of his records, where the full band would play, and then come down to just Louie and --
Yeah. Changed the texture of the rhythm section. And Jelly was the only one that you worked with that did that?
